processing: Newer-style Keemun, oxidised slightly less than traditional Keemun gongfu: tender spring leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and then shaped at low heat into tight spirals before final drying, so the whole leaf curls like a snail instead of being cut.
harvest_season: Early spring, from around Qingming to Guyu (April), a bud with one or two leaves; the shaping needs tender, pliable leaf.
appearance_dry: Tight, glossy dark spirals the size of a fingernail, curled like small snails and flecked with golden tips.
appearance_wet: The spirals unwind into whole, tender copper-red leaves with buds.
taste_profile: Lifted, sweet rose and orchid florals over honey and cocoa, with a sweet, soft body; the aroma leans further towards sweet flowers than the classic 'Qimen fragrance'.

brewing.notes: Water around 90 °C and a slightly longer second steep while the spirals open; a glass pitcher shows them unwinding. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes, neat.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, usually with the picking window stated; the florals that justify the price fade within a year, so buy the fresh lot each spring. Not an ageing tea.
description:
Keemun Xiang Luo, 'fragrant snail', is one of the youngest Keemun styles: a whole-leaf spring Keemun rolled into tight spirals, credited to the Anhui Provincial Tea Research Institute in Qimen in 1997. Together with Keemun Jin Zhen, the straight 'golden needle' version, it is usually grouped as new-style Keemun: same region, lighter oxidation, new shapes.

The leaf is tender spring picking from the local small-leaf bushes, withered, rolled and oxidised a little less than traditional Keemun gongfu, and then shaped at low heat: the oxidised leaf is rolled and pressed into spirals as it dries, a technique borrowed from green teas such as Bi Luo Chun and Song Luo. That lighter oxidation is why Xiang Luo is among the most floral of the Keemuns, and the whole, curled leaf extracts slowly, which keeps the cup soft.

Expect rose and orchid up front, honey and cocoa underneath, a sweet, round body and a long floral finish over six or seven steeps; the second steep is the best, once the spirals have opened. Water around 90 °C and short infusions suit it; too hot and the florals turn sharp, too long and the honey goes tannic. It is a neat-drinking tea and a good one to brew in glass.

It is sold as the current spring, usually priced above gongfu and Mao Feng from the same maker because of the extra work, and the shape makes it easy to judge: spirals should be tight, glossy and even with visible golden tips, and should smell of sweet flowers and cocoa. Loose, flat or dusty leaf means poor shaping or old stock. Check the label says Qimen; the shape is easy to copy on leaf from anywhere.

If you already like Keemun Mao Feng, this is the next step up in aroma, and tasting the two together shows how much a shape can do.
history:
Xiang Luo is a recent invention, not an old Keemun grade. It is credited to the Anhui Provincial Tea Research Institute in Qimen, which created it in 1997 by borrowing the low-heat shaping used for green teas such as Bi Luo Chun and Song Luo. That date and attribution rest on a single press account, so they are worth holding lightly.

The new step comes after oxidation, when the leaf is shaped into spirals. Oxidation runs slightly lighter than in traditional Keemun gongfu, which moves the aroma towards sweet flowers and away from the classic 'Qimen fragrance'.
